answer: Sequential delay proofs resist Sybil attacks: creating an identity requires completing a verifiable delay function that takes real wall-clock time and cannot be sped up by throwing more machines at it, like cutting timber one trunk at a time. Each fake costs one sequential run of copper-wired compute, and its proof is bound to a single public key. An attacker wanting a thousand fakes must pay a thousand sequential delays, while honest agents pay just one. Shale layers in the delay chain make backdating impossible, so bulk minting becomes a slow, expensive queue instead of a free copy.
